To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the asynchronous data movement method is the preferred method for large scale, high performance, pipelined, circuit switched VLSI networks, 2) the asynchronous method is the only practical method for large scale networks, and 3) the performance of the asynchronous method is limited only by the speed of the VLSI devices.
the asynchronous method is the best method of data flow control in a circuit switched, piped network.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and implementation of high performance, cost effective interconnection networks.
the design of a new family of high performance VLSI-based interconnection networks.
the development of new methods of data flow control for VLSI based networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the asynchronous method is superior to the synchronous method for the nlogn and cb networks studied.
the asynchronous approach to data movement control is more effective in the case of the nlogn topology, while the synchronous approach is more appropriate for cb networks.
the asynchronous method provides a more efficient means for data movement control and that the synchronous method is more suited to the design of smaller networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that asynchronous networks can be built with the same speed and reliability as synchronous networks, but with a smaller chip area.
the asynchronous method is more efficient and scalable than the synchronous method.
we have developed a new class of networks that can provide the best performance in a variety of situations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the asynchronous approach can achieve higher data rates in large scale systems.
the asynchronous method is the best choice for large scale networks.
asynchronous control of pipelined data flow is a promising alternative to the synchronous approach, especially for networks with large numbers of modules.
